name: Zane Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the studio by nine. It's four of us in a room above a bike shop: Ruth, who owns it, two other designers and me. Most days I'm doing menus, flyers and logos for cafés, a brewery, the summer street festival. I always start in my sketchbook with a pencil before I touch the computer, and Ruth teases me about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a logo clicks, when a café owner sees the sketch and says, yes, that's us. What wears me out is the endless rounds of changes for very little money. I earn less than most designers I studied with, and Lena, my partner, and I split rent on a small flat with less than a month's money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it was mostly hype. I'd probably post something smug about how clients still want a real person who listens. At the studio I'd be relieved out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI isn't my main problem even in this picture. We lost the brewery account in the spring to a cheaper freelancer, and Ruth has hinted she might cut us to four days. My pay is low and my savings are almost nothing, so the job already feels shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drawing and keep my head down at the studio. I'd ask Ruth straight out whether the four-day week is coming, so Lena and I can plan. I'd also start pitching the town's two new bakeries myself, to bring in work for the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief about the AI part, but not much more. It's the same tight feeling I have every month when the rent goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI isn't your main problem. What is the number that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss cuts us to four days, I lose about a fifth of my pay. That's roughly our food money for the month. There aren't other studios in this town I could walk into, maybe one, and it isn't hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI tools that do exist in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never used them and I don't want to. A lot of those tools were built on artists' work that nobody paid for, and I'm not going to help that along, even if it costs me a bit of time.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was overblown and clients still want a person who listens.
I'd say out loud at the studio that I'm **relieved**.
think: Privately, my job is **shaky** anyway, because the studio lost the **brewery account** in spring.
A **four-day week** would take about a fifth of my pay, which is our food money.
do: Ask Ruth (the studio owner) directly whether the **four-day week** is coming.
Pitch the town's **two new bakeries** to bring work into the studio.
Keep **sketching by hand** and never start using AI tools.
feel: **Relieved** about AI but still **tight** every month when the rent leaves.
S0.quote: If my boss cuts us to four days, I lose about a fifth of my pay. That's roughly our food money for the month.
fieldNote: Even in the mildest picture, Zane's worry comes from a **lost client** and low pay, not from AI.
He refuses AI on **principle**, because he believes it was built on unpaid artists' work.
There are **few studios** in his town, so a cut in hours has nowhere to go.

steps.text: Keep sketching logos and menus by hand at Ruth's studio
Pitch the two new bakeries in town for studio work
Ask Ruth whether the four-day week is coming before planning more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is theft dressed up as progress. Online I'd share every post about artists suing the AI companies. At the studio I'd argue that we should tell clients we don't use it, and make that our selling point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who gets squeezed out. Ruth can already see what those tools do with layouts and menus. If a café can get a logo from an app, the small jobs that pay my wage are gone first, and I'm the one who refuses the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the illustrators' and designers' union that's been trying to start up, and go to the meetings. I'd cancel the streaming subscriptions and the gym, which is about forty a month. And I'd talk to the sign painter on the high street about learning to paint shop fronts, because a brush on a wall isn't something a screen can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. And underneath that, scared, because I can't see where I'd land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools. If Ruth told you it was use them or leave, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably leave, and I know that sounds mad with no savings. Lena says I'm being stubborn. Maybe I'd last a month before I came back and asked for the job on her terms, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me, then Dev, who does most of the social media posts. His work is exactly the kind the tools do fastest. Ruth would keep whoever brings in clients and whoever uses the machines.

say: I'd say AI is **theft** dressed up as progress and back the **artists' lawsuits**.
I'd push the studio to sell itself as **made by people**.
think: I think I'm one of the first to be **squeezed out**, because I refuse the tools.
The **small jobs** that pay my wage, like café logos, go first.
do: Join the new **designers' union** and go to its meetings.
Cancel streaming and the gym to save about **forty a month**.
Ask the high street **sign painter** about learning to paint shop fronts.
feel: **Angry** at the AI companies, and underneath that **scared** of where he lands.
S1.quote: If a café can get a logo from an app, the small jobs that pay my wage are gone first, and I'm the one who refuses the tools.
fieldNote: Zane blames the **AI companies** and sees the fight as one about artists' rights.
He admits his **refusal** to use the tools makes him the easiest person to cut.
His escape route is **hands-on lettering**, which he hopes machines reach late.

steps.text: Join the designers' union that is starting up and attend meetings
Cancel streaming services and the gym membership, about forty a month
Ask the high street sign painter to teach shop-front lettering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments let this happen and they need to stop it, or at least pay people. I'd be at every protest outside the council and posting about a basic income. At work there wouldn't be much to say, because there'd barely be any work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my career would be over within a year or two. Design is all thinking and screen work, so it's gone on the first date, not three years later. The only part of me that's hands-on is the pencil, and nobody pays for a pencil sketch on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd go to the union and push for a fund for laid-off designers. I'd ask the sign painter to take me on even for nothing, just to learn while I can. Lena and I would probably give up the flat and move into her mum's spare room to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, really. I don't have a plan that works in two years, and I don't have the money to buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned signs. The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years after. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means painting shop fronts might give me three years, maybe. But three years of what, when every shop is closing too? I'd be learning a trade right as the thing that kills it is on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm sorry, and that I should have listened about learning the tools. Then I'd tell her we're moving to her mum's, because I can't make the rent. I think she'd be kinder about it than I deserve.

say: I'd say **governments** let this happen and must stop it or **pay people**.
I'd join **protests** at the council and post about a **basic income**.
think: I think my career is **over** within a year or two.
Design is **screen work**, so it goes on the **first date**, not three years later.
do: Push the union for a **fund** for laid-off designers.
Learn **sign painting** for free while there's still time.
Give up the flat and move into **Lena's mum's** spare room.
feel: **Panicked**, with no workable plan and **no money** to buy time.
S2.quote: Design is all thinking and screen work, so it's gone on the first date, not three years later.
fieldNote: Zane sees his job as almost entirely **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help.
His **hands-on trade** idea feels pointless to him with only three years of runway.
He admits regret about **refusing the tools**, which he hadn't said before.

steps.text: Push the union to set up a fund for laid-off designers
Protest at the council for a basic income
Learn sign painting from the high street painter, unpaid if needed
Give up the flat and move into Lena's mum's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: this needs rules and it needs a union. With five years there's time to actually pass something. I'd be the person handing out leaflets at the design meetups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just enough to change trades if I start this week. Five years isn't enough if I keep telling myself it won't happen. The trouble is that I'm slow to change, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the sign-writing evening course at the college, which is about three hundred for the term. I'd ask Ruth to let me do four days so I can apprentice on the fifth. I'd put twenty a week aside, even if it's only twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a bit of air in it. Like the floor is tilting rather than falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the three hundred for the course come from, with less than a month saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my old drawing tablet and the second monitor, which I'd hardly need anyway. That's most of it. The rest I'd pay off over a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After robots arrive in 2034, what's left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe nothing. I'd be thirty-five and starting again, and I'd want there to be a public jobs scheme or something, because I won't have savings to fall back on.

say: I'd say this needs **rules** and a **union**, and five years is time to pass them.
I'd hand out **leaflets** at the local design meetups.
think: Five years is **just enough** to change trades if I start this week.
My problem is that I'm **slow to change**, and I know it.
do: Sign up for the **sign-writing** evening course, about **three hundred** a term.
Ask for a **four-day week** to apprentice on the fifth day.
Save **twenty a week**, even if it's only that.
feel: **Worried** but with a little air, like the floor is **tilting** rather than falling.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough to change trades if I start this week. Five years isn't enough if I keep telling myself it won't happen.
fieldNote: Zane names his own **resistance to change** as the main risk.
He would fund retraining by **selling equipment**, which shows how thin his cushion is.
After the robot date he has **no plan** and hopes for a public jobs scheme.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's sign-writing evening course this year
Put twenty a week into a savings jar
Cut to four days at Ruth's studio to apprentice on the fifth
Hand out union leaflets at the local design meetups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years, so let's use them to protect people, not just shareholders. I'd keep pushing the union line. I'd tell friends to start learning a trade now, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking part lands and forty when robots do. That's time to become a proper sign painter and build some regular customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do nothing dramatic. I'd keep the studio job and do the evening course, and maybe paint one shop front for a friend for practice. Lena and I would try to save a month of rent by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. A decade is long enough for me to stop being stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing dramatic. Is that a plan or is that waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. A bit of both, if I'm honest. I tend to wait until I'm forced, so I'd want the course booked by January or I'd never do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change any big plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids in a few years. I think we'd still want them, but I'd want to know I have a trade first. So maybe it gets pushed back a bit.

say: I'd say ten years should be used to **protect people**, not just shareholders.
I'd tell friends to start learning a **trade** now.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**, since I'd be **thirty-seven** when thinking AI lands.
That's enough time to build **regular customers** as a sign painter.
do: Keep the **studio job** and take the evening course alongside it.
Paint **one shop front** for a friend as practice.
Save **one month of rent** by the end of the year.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to breathe, because a **decade** beats his own stubbornness.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough for me to stop being stubborn.
fieldNote: With a decade, Zane shifts from protest to a slow, **realistic plan**.
He knows he tends to **wait until forced**, and sets himself a January deadline.
Plans for **children** are pushed back until he has a trade.

steps.text: Book the sign-writing course by January while keeping the studio job
Save one month of rent by the end of the year
Put off having children until the sign trade pays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years and I've got nothing, no savings, no other skill that pays. What would help is a public fund that pays people like me to retrain, and a proper union for designers so we're not each alone with our bosses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. If a client pays an app instead of me, that money goes to some company far away, not to anyone in this town. That's the part that makes me angriest.

headlineQuote: If a client pays an app instead of me, that money goes to some company far away, not to anyone in this town.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old designer** at a four-person studio, earning low pay with less than a month saved.
He sketches every job **by hand first** and refuses AI tools on principle.
He blames **AI companies** and governments, and turns to a union and protest as his first response.
As warning time grows, he moves from **panic** to a slow plan to become a **sign painter**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd have no savings and no other skill that pays.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** to pay for retraining, and a proper **designers' union**.
